## PROP  
 3

## PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. **Fiscal Impact**: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. **Supporters**: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA **Opponents**: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

### WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS

YES A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.

 

### ARGUMENTS

PRO PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.

CON Californians *already pay* the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes *temporary income taxes permanent* while Sacramento *wastes billions* on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. *Fix spending first* before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

### FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

FOR

## PROP  
 3

## PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax.*** The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.

***Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases.*** Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.

***How Does the State Spend Its Money?*** This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.

### PROPOSAL

Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year.*** The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.

***Funding for Education and Other Programs.*** Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

## PROP  
 3

## PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3

PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE AND OUR COMMUNITIES WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES.

Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone. Prop. 3 prevents millionaires and billionaires from getting a tax cut, and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms.

PROP. 3 PREVENTS BILLIONS IN CUTS TO OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE.

Without Prop. 3, California’s 8 million public school and community college students face billions in cuts, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes. Families could lose access to preventive healthcare and affordable prescription drugs, and the Medi-Cal coverage that millions of Californians rely on could be put at risk.

PROP. 3 ONLY EXTENDS THE CURRENT TAX RATES ON THE WEALTHIEST TOP 2%.

Prop. 3 maintains the income tax rates that the wealthiest Californians have paid for the past 15 years. If those tax rates are allowed to expire, it would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities. Proposition 3 keeps the existing rates on the top 2% of incomes.

GUARANTEES THE MONEY REACHES THE CLASSROOM— NOT SACRAMENTO.

Proposition 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability. It guarantees that funds from Proposition 3 go directly to local schools—the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it, redirect it, or spend a single dollar on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Prop. 3’s school guarantee then frees up billions that help fund Medi-Cal for children, seniors and families.

Every dollar in Prop. 3 is independently audited every year and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties. Local school districts must post annual accounting online to guarantee that Californians know exactly how and where funds are spent.

PROP. 3 SECURES OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE.

For more than a decade, these revenues have helped fund critical programs California families and communities count on—from school lunches, smaller class sizes and mental health counselors to children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal. They’ve also helped stave off cuts during economic downturns by investing more in the state’s Rainy Day Fund, protecting our schools and healthcare when the economy slows. Proposition 3 keeps that progress going for the next generation.

PROP. 3 IS SUPPORTED BY TEACHERS, NURSES, AND HEALTHCARE WORKERS.

Yes on 3 is supported by: 

*   California State PTA
*   California Federation of Teachers
*   California Nurses Association
*   California School Employees Association
*   California School Nurses Organization
*   California Teachers Association
*   Community College League of California
*   Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
*   Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA

The educators in our classrooms and the nurses who care for our kids all agree: Vote YES on Proposition 3. Let’s protect what matters most, without raising your taxes. Vote YES on Proposition 3.

*www.YesProp3CA.com*

**David Goldberg**, President  
 California Teachers Association  
 **Katie Nilsson**, RN, President  
 California School Nurses Organization  
 **Jodi Hicks**, President  
 Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3

NO ON PROP. 3—STOP PERMANENTLY HIGHER INCOME TAXES

In 2012, politicians and special interests promised Californians that their income tax increases would be TEMPORARY. Now they’re claiming that making those taxes permanent somehow ISN’T a tax increase at all. Don’t buy it. Prop. 3 locks in what would become the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history— costing taxpayers up to $15 billion every year.

NO ON PROP. 3—REMIND POLITICIANS WHAT “TEMPORARY” MEANS

*Temporary: lasting for a limited time only; not permanent.*

California taxpayers kept their end of the bargain—paying temporary higher income taxes for 16 years. Politicians should keep theirs and stop pushing for even higher taxes.

NO ON PROP. 3—STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING

Prop. 3 does nothing to stop the waste, fraud and reckless spending that turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion deficit in just three years. If Sacramento had spent responsibly, they wouldn’t be asking taxpayers to make “temporary” taxes permanent.

NO ON PROP. 3—DON’T MAKE CALIFORNIA EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE

Californians have the highest cost of living and pay the highest income, sales and gas taxes in America. Making a temporary tax permanent only makes California more expensive.

NO ON PROP. 3—FIX THE SPENDING PROBLEM FIRST

California doesn’t have a tax revenue problem—it has a spending problem. California’s population grew by less than 2% in the past decade while the politicians doubled spending. Say no to permanently higher taxes. Join us to oppose higher income taxes at *VoteNoProp3.com*.

NO ON PROP. 3

**Jon Coupal**, President  
 Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association  
 **Carlos Solorzano**, CEO  
 Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco  
 **Clint Olivier**, President  
 Central Valley Business Federation

### ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 3

PROP. 3—TURNS “TEMPORARY” TAXES INTO PERMANENT HIGHER INCOME TAXES

Sacramento politicians make big promises to get our support for higher taxes. Then they spend our tax dollars with no accountability—losing billions to waste, fraud and overspending.

Take Prop. 3. Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary—only for seven years to cover a budget deficit. Then those “temporary” taxes were extended for another 12 years with the promise to voters that the higher taxes would solve the problems the politicians created. Now the special interests and politicians want to make these higher income taxes PERMANENT.

California voters should say NO to PERMANENTLY higher income taxes.

PROP. 3—HIGHER INCOME TAXES = HIGHER COST OF LIVING

Californians have the nation’s highest cost of living partly because we also suffer from the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes of all fifty states. The same politicians also gave us the highest gasoline prices in the nation, higher insurance costs, higher utility costs, higher food costs, and higher housing costs. Now they want to make higher income taxes permanent, while adding new taxes on your health insurance, new taxes on software—and they are even considering a “jobs” tax. Say NO to INCREASING our cost of living with higher taxes.

PROP. 3—VOTERS DESERVE REAL RESULTS, NOT BROKEN PROMISES

Waste, fraud and overspending by state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.

The politicians and special interests promised temporary income taxes were needed to avoid big cuts to government programs. Since the “temporary” increases were first passed, government spending has increased by $150 billion—a more than 2.5X increase. Over the same time period, our schools, infrastructure and public safety have gotten worse. Say NO to endless broken promises.

NO ON PROP. 3—STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING

The politicians and special interests turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years. They mismanaged our tax dollars so badly, they now want voters to bail them out with permanently higher taxes.

Say NO to $100 billion wasted on a train to nowhere.

Say NO to $37 billion wasted on homeless programs that don’t work.

Say NO to $31 billion wasted on unemployment fraud.

NO ON PROP. 3—FIX SACRAMENTO’S SPENDING PROBLEM BEFORE RAISING TAXES

California doesn’t have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem. California’s population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.

It’s not just state taxes that keep going up. Politicians and special interests have imposed more than 2,000 new local tax increases in just the past ten years—making it much harder for struggling Californians to make ends meet.

Californians shouldn’t support any higher taxes until we get spending under control.

STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING.

NO NEW TAXES.

NO ON PROP. 3.

**Robert Gutierrez**, President  
 California Taxpayers Association  
 **Robert Rivinius**, President  
 Family Business Association of California  
 **Julian Canete**, President  
 California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST  
PROPOSITION 3

Proposition 3 protects our schools, our healthcare and our communities—without raising your taxes.

PROP. 3 KEEPS THE TAX RATES THE TOP 2% HAVE PAID FOR THE PAST 15 YEARS AND DOES NOT RAISE YOUR TAXES.

Prop. 3 maintains the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% of Californians have been paying for 15 years, ensuring couples that earn more than $740,000 continue to pay their fair share.

WITHOUT PROP. 3 MILLIONAIRES AND BILLIONAIRES GET A MASSIVE TAX CUT—AND THE REST OF US PAY FOR IT.

Teacher and staff layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and fewer counselors in our schools; cuts to Medi-Cal, children’s healthcare and the clinics families rely on; and less for the firefighters, emergency response and wildfire protection that keep our communities safe.

PROP. 3 HAS STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND FUNDS EDUCATION DIRECTLY.

Prop. 3’s funding goes straight to local schools and community colleges. Sacramento politicians cannot touch it or redirect it. Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Every dollar is independently audited every year, districts must post their spending online, and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties.

PROP. 3 PROTECTS HEALTHCARE AND FIRE PROTECTION.

By guaranteeing funding for our classrooms, Prop. 3 ensures California can also invest in Medi-Cal and children’s healthcare, and in the firefighters and wildfire protection our communities depend on. That’s why teachers, school employees, nurses and firefighters agree: VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 3.

*www.YesProp3CA.com* 

**Jeff Freitas**, President  
 California Federation of Teachers  
 **Darrell Roberts**, President  
 California Professional Firefighters  
 **Adam Weinberger**, President  
 California School Employees Association

## PROP  
 3

## PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

  

### OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY

### PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL

*   Makes permanent the existing 2012 voter-approved tax rates for high-income Californians, currently set to expire in 2031.
*   Rates apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers, and $505,000 for heads of household (2025 levels; adjusted annually for inflation).
*   Allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges.
*   Allows local school boards to decide how revenues are spent; bars use for administrative costs.
*   Increases General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves, and other programs.

### SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:

*   Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

# Should Voters Approve Prop. 3? How Top Tax Rates Have Helped Californians

A Look at What California's Top Tax Rates Have Funded — and What's at Risk if Voters Don't Approve Prop. 3

July 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center

Print Report 

![A young child wearing a blue backpack hugs and adult's waist outside a school building, capturing a quiet moment during school drop-off.](https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2026/07/iStock-2169109359.webp) 

### key takeaway

Proposition 3 will appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot, asking California voters whether to make permanent the higher-income tax rates on the state’s highest earners. These top tax rates were first enacted by voters in 2012 and renewed in 2016 to help fund schools, health care, and other supports for working families. Without action, the current rates are set to expire after 2030, reducing state revenues by billions of dollars annually and threatening funding for schools and state programs and services that support Californians every day.

### table of Contents

*   [What Would Prop. 3 Do?](#h-what-would-prop-3-do)
*   [Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55](#h-background-on-prop-30-and-prop-55)
*   [Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?](#h-who-pays-the-voter-approved-top-tax-rates)
*   [Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Credit](#h-without-voter-approved-tax-rates-the-top-1-would-receive-another-tax-cut)
*   [Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared](#h-top-earners-incomes-have-soared)
*   [What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?](#h-what-have-the-top-income-tax-rates-accomplished)
*   [Why Renewing the Top Tax Rates Matters for California](#h-why-renewing-the-top-tax-rates-matters-for-california)

## **What Would Prop. 3 Do?**

Prop. 3  would make permanent the rates put in place since 2012, preserving a key element of progressivity (requiring households with higher incomes to pay higher tax rates) in the state’s revenue structure that funds critical investments that improve the quality of life for all Californians. The measure would not raise taxes or change existing income tax rates; it simply removes the expiration date on current tax rates for the state’s highest earners. Revenues would continue to support the entire state General Fund budget by helping meet the TK-14 constitutional funding guarantee and freeing up revenue for other programs and services, just as they have since 2012.

## **Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55**

In 2012, after the state faced significant revenue losses as a result of the Great Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which added new income tax brackets for the state’s highest earners (10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3%, depending on household income) and included a temporary sales tax increase. Both the income tax rates and the sales tax increase were temporary, with the sales tax set to expire in 2016 and the income tax rates in 2018. Proposition 30 also created the Education Protection Account, a state account in the General Fund that receives and disburses revenues from the top income tax rates.

### what is the education protection account (epa)?

*Proposition 30 (2012) established the Education Protection Account, a state account where revenues from the top income tax rates are deposited. Of the funds in the account, 89% are distributed to schools and 11% to community colleges. This revenue is treated as General Fund revenue, subject to constitutional requirements including Prop. 98 (1988), the state’s minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education, and Prop. 2 (2014), which established rules for building state budget reserves and paying down state debts. The revenue deposited into the EPA increases the Prop. 98 guarantee and is used to help meet the guarantee, freeing up General Fund revenue for other state budget priorities.*

In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended the income tax rates for another 12 years (to 2030), while allowing the sales tax to expire as scheduled. Prop. 55 also added a [constitutional formula intended to increase funding for the Medi-Cal program](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3765) when revenues exceed a certain threshold. This specific formula has never directed funds to Medi-Cal, and the current measure would allow it to expire. However, top tax rate revenues do support the Medi-Cal budget indirectly through the General Fund capacity generated by Prop. 55.

Since their initial enactment in 2012, these higher tax rates have generated around $120 billion for schools and other essential services. In recent years, the higher rates have generated around $10 billion annually. These revenues now form a core component of the state budget, supporting the TK-14 education budget, strengthening General Fund capacity to support other vital programs and services, and building reserves.

## **Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?**

**The voter-approved top tax rates only impact the highest-income Californians.**

These rates only apply to the [top 2% of California tax filers](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016). In tax year 2025, these top rates only applied to people with incomes above around $371,000 for single tax filers and about $743,000 for married couples filing jointly. These thresholds increase annually with inflation.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/0ETiu/full.png) 

## **Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Cut**

**The top-earning 1% of Californians would receive a major tax cut if Prop. 55 rates are not extended.** If the voter-approved top tax rates are allowed to expire, the vast majority of tax filers in the top 1% by income would receive an average annual tax cut of nearly $59,000, according to estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. This top 1% group would get about 98% of the total tax cuts. The remaining tax cuts would go to some households in the next 4% of highest-income filers.[1](javascript:void\(0\))Not all households in the top 5% or top 1% would receive tax cuts from the expiration of the top tax rates for several reasons. First, filers are subject to the top tax rates if their *taxable income* — that is, income after accounting for allowed exemptions and deductions — exceeds the thresholds established by Prop. 30 and Prop. 50. In contrast, the thresholds for the top 5% and top 1% used by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for this analysis are based on *total income* before exemptions and deductions. So tax filers in the top 1% by total income may have taxable incomes under the threshold for the top rates. Second, some high-income filers that use specific tax preferences may be subject to an “alternative minimum tax,” which could be triggered if their regular tax bill were reduced. And finally, because thresholds for these rates vary by household type, a married couple filing a joint tax return with a total income of $500,000 falls into the top 5% of all tax filers, but their total income — even before accounting for exemptions and deductions — is below the threshold for the Prop. 55 taxes of around $743,000, for example. Around 15% of this group would receive a tax cut, averaging more than $2,000 annually. Californians in all other income groups would see no change to their taxes.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/9oM4q/full.png) 

**California’s tax system would be more regressive if the Prop. 55 tax rates expire.** A [regressive tax system](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/) is one in which lower-income households pay larger shares of their income in taxes than higher-income households. In contrast, in a progressive tax system, higher-income people pay higher shares of their income in taxes. California’s tax system is [more progressive than many other state tax systems](https://itep.org/whopays-7th-edition/), in large part due to these voter-approved top tax rates that are up for renewal under Prop. 3.

When you add up the various state and local taxes that Californians pay — including the sales tax, property tax, and other types of taxes — the highest-income 1% currently pay about 12% of their income in taxes on average. That’s barely more than the 11.7% paid by Californians in the lowest 20% by income. If the top rates were not in effect, the top 1% would pay only about 10.7% of their income in state and local taxes — *lower* than what the bottom fifth of Californians pay.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/uErxw/full.png) 

## **Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared**

**The number of Californians with incomes high enough to be subject to the voter-approved top tax rates has more than doubled, reflecting soaring incomes among top earners.** Around 185,000 tax filers, including more than 175,000 California resident filers, had incomes above the thresholds for Prop. 30’s top tax rates in 2013, the first year the rates were in effect. By 2024 (the latest available data), the number had reached nearly 376,000, including around 355,000 California residents.[2](javascript:void\(0\))“Tax filer” represents a tax filing unit — the primary filer as well as any spouses and dependents included on the tax return. A tax filing unit can be an individual, a couple, or a family, and in some cases can include unrelated dependents. This increase is due to the incomes of these high-income households growing much faster than inflation over this period.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Cacwj/full.png) 

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OJ1v4/full.png) 

**Californians subject to the top tax rates have seen their incomes grow dramatically over the past several decades, while most Californians have lost ground or experienced income declines** *after adjusting for inflation*. The top 1% of Californians saw their inflation-adjustedincomes increase more than 2.5 times (157%) between 1987 and 2024, while those in the bottom 80% saw decreases in real income over that time.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/4iSlI/full.png) 

To be in the top 1%, a tax filer had an income of at least $973,097 in 2024. On average, this group reported more than $3 million per tax return in 2024 — about 54 times the income of the middle fifth of Californians, who earned around $56,000 on average. In even starker contrast, the top 0.1% had an average income of over $15 million — 268 times that of the middle fifth of Californians. In other words, someone in the top 1% can earn in just under one week what the average middle-income Californian earns in an entire year, and someone in the top 0.1% can earn that amount in *just over a day*.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/vt1Tg/full.png) 

## **What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?**

Since the passage of Prop. 30 in 2012, the top tax rates have generated about $120 billion in state revenue.[3](javascript:void\(0\))This figure reflects revenues from the top tax rates allocated to TK-14 education from the Education Protection Account (EPA) through the 2024-25 fiscal year. On average, this revenue has represented about 5.5% of total General Fund revenues. The funds raised by the top tax rates approved by voters through Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have been a major revenue source for the state, supporting critical services including education, health care, and economic security programs. This revenue has also helped the state to build up budget reserves to be better prepared for downturns when revenues decline or come in lower than expected.

**The annual revenue raised by the top tax rates has increased in line with overall state revenues**. These revenues are sensitive to stock market fluctuations, as a large share of the income of high-income households comes from earnings on investments such as dividends and capital gains. For example, Prop. 55 revenues peaked at more than $16 billion when the stock market surged in 2021 and then subsequently fell in line with the stock market decline in the following years, before growing to nearly $12 billion in 2024. The sensitivity of these revenues to economic conditions makes it all the more important that state leaders have the capacity to save revenues during high-revenue years in the state’s budget reserves for future downturns, as required under [Prop. 2 of 2014](https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/140924_Proposition_2_BB.pdf) — which may be modified to require additional savings in some strong-revenue years if voters approve changes to the existing measure with Prop. 2 on the November 2026 ballot.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yNptb/full.png) 

**Top tax rate revenues provide critical support for schools and community colleges**. Top tax rate revenues serve two purposes for the TK-14 education budget: 1) increase the Prop. 98 minimum guarantee’s annual calculation and 2) provide the revenues needed to meet the guarantee. Because top tax rate revenues count as General Fund revenues, they directly affect how the annual Prop. 98 level is calculated. In years when the General Fund experiences strong growth, the guarantee is set as a share (about 40%) of General Fund revenues, establishing a higher floor.[4](javascript:void\(0\))The minimum guarantee is determined using one of three formulas: 1) approximately 40% of General Fund revenue, 2) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and growth in per capita personal income, or 3) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and per capita General Fund revenue growth. In other years, the guarantee builds on the prior year’s level, carrying forward the growth built when revenues were strong. Regardless of how the guarantee is calculated, the effect of the top tax rate revenue is cumulative. As shown in the chart below, the guarantee has grown on an ongoing basis since 2012-13, with part of this growth attributable to the top tax rates.

### what is proposition 98?

*Prop. 98 is a constitutional amendment adopted by California voters in 1988 that establishes an annual minimum funding level for TK-14 education each fiscal year, commonly referred to as the minimum guarantee. Prop. 98 funding comes from a combination of state General Fund revenue and local property taxes. Prop. 98 spending supports TK-12 schools, community colleges, county offices of education, the state preschool program, and state agencies that provide direct TK-14 instructional programs. While Prop. 98 establishes a required minimum funding level for programs falling under the guarantee as a whole, it does not protect individual programs from reduction or elimination.*

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/9GMeB/full.png) 

In addition to raising the guarantee’s calculation, Prop. 55 revenues directly help meet the guarantee. Revenues from the top tax rates are used to meet the Prop. 98 obligation, which frees up General Fund dollars that would otherwise be needed to meet the guarantee. These freed-up dollars are used to support non-TK-14 programs, build state reserves, and pay down debts. Since 2012-13, when these revenues began to flow to schools and community colleges, Prop. 55 revenues have provided about $120 billion to help meet the TK-14 budget.[5](javascript:void\(0\))While the top tax rate revenues have provided approximately $120 billion to the TK-14 budget through the EPA, because these revenues also reduce the General Fund dollars to meet the guarantee, the overall education funding impact is approximately 40% of total revenues.

The chart below shows the growth in the minimum guarantee, and the share provided by the top tax rate revenues, adjusted to 2024 dollars. Throughout this period, top tax rate revenues have enabled the state to implement key educational programs. For example, in the 2013-14 school year, policymakers began implementing [a major school finance reform](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4108/download?inline&file=CA_LCFF_School_Funding_Effectiveness_REPORT.pdf) to more equitably allocate dollars to school districts based on student need.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/I6ljL/full.png) 

*   [Top tax rate revenues have also created more General Fund capacity to support critical economic security, housing, and health programs.](#block_7cc3a46c1340f8596050a225c0b9db86-section-0)
*   [Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have increased the state’s capacity to save for a rainy day and pay down debts.](#block_7cc3a46c1340f8596050a225c0b9db86-section-1)

Top tax rate revenues have also created more General Fund capacity to support critical economic security, housing, and health programs.

By helping meet the TK-14 constitutional funding guarantee, these revenues reduce General Fund dollars needed for that obligation, freeing up resources for other budget priorities, including: 

*   [California’s Earned Income Tax Credit](https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/caleitc/), which boosts incomes for workers who earn little from their jobs, was initially established in 2015, and was expanded to more Californians in 2017 and 2018.
*   In 2021, policymakers launched a multi-year plan to fund an increase of 200,000 child care slots, reaching about 152,000 in 2026-27, making progress in expanding access to children and families with low incomes.
*   In 2019, the state created the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) program, which provides funding to localities to finance solutions tailored to their needs and has shown positive outcomes, [including reducing youth homelessness](https://jbay.org/resources/investing-in-impact-2025/).
*   Policymakers restored several Medi-Cal benefits between 2014 and 2019 that had been cut due to budget shortfalls during the Great Recession, including adult dental benefits, podiatry, optometry, audiology, and speech therapy services**.**
*   The state has made progress on reducing deep poverty among families with children by increasing [CalWORKs cash grants](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/the-role-of-calworks-in-alleviating-deep-poverty/), and reducing poverty among older adults and people with disabilities by increasing [Supplemental Security Income/State Supplementary Payment (SSI/SSP) grants](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/ssi-ssp-grants-moving-in-the-right-direction-but-still-not-enough/), after both programs had been subject to deep cuts during the Great Recession.

Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have increased the state’s capacity to save for a rainy day and pay down debts.

The revenues from the top tax rates have helped put the state in a better position to weather difficult economic times by increasing deposits into state budget reserves and helping to pay down budgetary debt.[6](javascript:void\(0\))Prop. 2 (2026), if approved, would make additional changes to require state leaders to increase deposits into the rainy day fund in some high-revenue years. Voters approved Prop. 2 in 2014, which requires the state to set aside a certain share of General Fund revenues each year in order to build the state’s rainy day fund (the [Budget Stabilization Account](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-budget-stabilization-account-bsa-california-s-largest-reserve)) and pay down state budgetary debts. Under these rules, the state must set aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year, half of which is deposited into the rainy day fund while the other half must be used to pay down state debts.[7](javascript:void\(0\))Starting in 2030-31, the entire amount will be deposited into the rainy day fund, although  policymakers will retain the option to use up to one-half to pay down debts. Additionally, the state is required to set aside additional revenues in years when revenues from taxes on capital gains exceed 8% of total General Fund tax revenues.

Since Prop. 2, California has been able to build up substantial reserves, aided by the revenues generated by Prop. 30 and Prop. 55. The balance is projected to be more than $15 billion for fiscal year 2026-27 under the enacted budget. In addition to the required 1.5% set-aside of revenues, Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have likely resulted in larger capital gains-related set-asides, as high-income people subject to the top tax rates receive more of their income in the form of capital gains (proceeds from selling assets such as stock holdings).

Prop. 2 also created a new budget reserve to support schools and community colleges, the [Public School System Stabilization Account](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-public-school-system-stabilization-account-psssa-the-reserve-for-k-12-schools-amp-community-colleges) (PSSSA). Deposits into this reserve are required only if certain budget conditions are met, typically when revenue growth is strong — particularly revenue from capital gains. Thus, the top tax rates help to boost deposits into this reserve to support TK-14 education when revenues fall short.

In recent years, the PSSSA has provided one-time resources to sustain education programs. For example, in the 2023-24 fiscal year, the state was not able to meet the minimum guarantee and the full balance ($8.4 billion) was withdrawn to help sustain existing programs. At the end of 2026-27, the mandatory deposits in this account are projected to total $8.7 billion, with a full balance of $9.4 billion. 

## **Why Renewing the Top Tax Rates Matters for California**

As the revenues from the current top tax rates have become a critical source of funding for education, health care, and other state services, their expiration after 2030 would likely lead to significant budget shortfalls. If Prop. 3 does not pass — and state leaders or voters do not approve alternative revenues — funding for essential state services would be put in jeopardy. This is especially concerning given that state officials already project ongoing budget deficits in upcoming years, as the cost of existing state services is growing due to inflation and a changing population, and revenue growth is not keeping up. Those projected deficits, compounded by [federal cuts resulting from H.R. 1](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” would put significant pressure on the state budget and the programs it supports.

In recent years, the top tax rates have contributed around $10 billion annually to the state budget, and the Legislative Analyst’s Office projects that making these rates permanent would bring in between [$5 billion and $15 billion annually](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016) in the future — depending on the economy and stock market performance. The loss of $5 billion to $15 billion could mean:

*   **Reduced General Fund resources to protect and strengthen services that keep Californians healthy, housed, and economically secure**. In recent years, more than [two-thirds of state spending growth](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5176) from available revenues has gone simply to sustaining existing levels of services, including keeping pace with rising costs and growing caseloads in programs like Medi-Cal, In-Home Supportive Services, and child care. The loss of Prop. 55 revenues would worsen existing deficit projections, making it harder for the state to maintain even current levels of services, potentially leading to programmatic cuts to essential programs.
*   **The loss of a key revenue stream and increased pressure to meet the Prop. 98 minimum guarantee.** In the near term, without the revenues from the top tax rates, the state would need to replace billions in funding for TK-12 education from other General Fund sources to meet the guarantee, potentially resulting in cuts to other services like health care and child care.[8](javascript:void\(0\))As noted in a text box above (“What Is the Education Protection Account?”), the revenues from the top tax rates both 1) increase the Prop. 98 guarantee and 2) are used to help meet the guarantee, freeing up General Fund revenue for other state budget priorities. If the top tax rates are not extended, the revenues that they generate would be eliminated after the 2030 tax year. This would *impact the level* of the Prop. 98 guarantee while also *creating a hole* in the Prop. 98 budget that would have to be filled with other General Fund revenue. In the long run, the loss of this dedicated revenue stream would result in the Prop. 98 guarantee being lower than if the top tax rates were extended — by around 40% of the total revenue loss. In other words, TK-14 education would receive less funding over time than it would if voters extended the top rates.
*   **A reduced capacity to save and prepare for economic downturns.** Without the additional revenues from the current top tax rates, deposits into the state’s rainy day fund and debt repayments required by Prop. 2 would be lower. This would leave the state less resilient when the next recession arrives, making critical state services more vulnerable to cuts.
*   **Diminished ability to respond to anticipated federal cuts.** The 2025 budget reconciliation package, H.R.1, includes significant cuts to health care and food assistance. Cuts to health care could total tens of billions each year. On top of that, cuts to food assistance could cost the state more than $5 billion annually. Currently, the state budget does not have the General Fund capacity to fully address these cuts, and the loss of top tax rates would only increase the millions of Californians at risk of losing these critical services.

## Key Findings

Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.

These are the key findings of the *Californians and their Government* survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:

*   **Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.** Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
*   **Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label.** Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
*   **![Figure - Top state issues chosen by Californians](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/survey-1026_key-findings_fig1.png)Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today.** Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
*   **![Figure - Top national issues chosen by Californians](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='385'%20height='149'%20viewBox='0%200%20385%20149'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today.** Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.

## November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures

Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.

**Gubernatorial Election.** California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our [July survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.

![Figure - Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton by a wide margin in the governor's race](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='652'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20652'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% [October 2022 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/)), and the 2018 general election (60% [October 2018 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).

About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in [October 2022](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in [October 2018](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.

**House Races.** When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in [September](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), [July](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).

![Figure - A solid majority of California likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate if the 2026 election for the House of Representatives were held today](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='644'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20644'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in [May,](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in [September 2024](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

**Legislative Ballot Measures.** We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.

*   **Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs).** Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
*   **Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund).** Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
*   **Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns).** Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
*   **Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers).** Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
*   **Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services).** Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 43 varies across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).

![Table - Majorities of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 1 (Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (Rainy Day Fund)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1622'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201622'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot

In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).

After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).

![Figure - A majority of California likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='596'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20596'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.

A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.

Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).

Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.

![Figure - Fifty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote no on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='596'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20596'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.

A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.

Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.

Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.

![Table - About half of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit) and Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1718'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201718'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## State of the State

Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.

When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.

Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since [June 2023](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.

![Figure - A majority of Californians think things in the state are generally going in the wrong direction](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='978'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20978'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.

With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).

![Figure - Three in four feel their income is not keeping up with inflation](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='852'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20852'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since [October 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.

Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last [October](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.

When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.

![Table - More Californians approve of Governor Newsom than of the state legislature or their own legislators](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1578'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201578'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## State of the Nation

Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.

A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October [ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.

![Figure - Eight in ten Californians think things in the nation are generally going in the wrong direction](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='978'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20978'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.

Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.

When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.

![Figure - Most Californians are not satisfied with how democracy is working in the United States](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='638'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20638'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in [October 2018](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.

Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since [June 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.

Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.

Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October [Reuters/Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.

Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since [October 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.

About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from [October 2024](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

![Table - Three in ten or fewer Californians approve of the president, the US Congress, and their own House representative](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1546'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201546'%3E%3C/svg%3E)
